Meaning, yes. He accepted the name.

Jouansai Yagyuu.
Current head of Yagyuu Shinkage-ryuu's Rokuhara branch, the martial art the shogunate kept strictly within its own gates. Sword instructor to the shogunate army. Commander of the Stable Corps, the Ashikaga family's personal guard...

In short: Yamato's number one swordsman. Number one only.

He explained with the expression of a teacher who took good care of his pupils.

This particular pupil was not understanding even half.

Start late, then make up the loss with efficient swordwork—no, not merely make it up. Get ahead instead.

That much had entered my head. Beyond that, admission was closed.
I could neither copy it nor think how to defeat it.

en.html:
Muramasa wanted me to consider our full arsenal. Ending—the Railgun—included.

For this red tsurugi, even proposing it must have been humiliating. Full strength, against one unarmored human!

But pride was not why I refused.

No more killing by me. By Muramasa.
That was my promise to Ichijou: keep the curse asleep, the curse that killed even good, innocent people.

Use every ability of the tsurugi, and I would kill him. No avoiding it. Killing was precisely what a tsurugi was built for.

I had chosen to follow Ichijou. On that oath, I had to hold back.

en.html:
Nothing but provocation, those words. Yet his tone was so mild it did not sound provocative at all. Black machinery covered his eyes. What he really intended, I could not see either.

Still, the problem he had presented was my reality exactly. No exaggeration required.
One opponent. One of me. But decisive reinforcements were coming for him, and none for me.

His sword had reached the innermost secrets of Yagyuu Shinkage-ryuu, a great school at the summit of this country's martial history. Kageaki Minato had just about mastered one obscure school.

Both were swords, yes. The weight behind them was another matter.
The supposedly absolute advantage of a warrior over bare flesh might as well not exist.

Now what?
How was I to break this situation open?
